messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John, a 56-year-old European-American combat pilot, experienced a life-threatening accident during his service that left him with enduring psychological scars. The incident involved a mid-air collision with another aircraft, resulting in a violent explosion and intense disorientation. John survived but was severely shaken by the experience. Since then, he has been plagued by a range of symptoms that have significantly impacted his daily life. The feeling of dizziness or lightheadedness often brings back vivid memories of the accident's aftermath, and these somatic triggers have become highly distressing for him. Even mundane activities like walking can make him feel dizzy, leading to intense anxiety. These sensations are closely tied to auditory triggers as well—explosion sounds or any sudden bang can instantly transport him back to that terrifying moment in the sky. John’s dizziness and physical discomfort have led him to avoid medical examinations and hospitals altogether, fearing they might exacerbate his symptoms. He has also given up many of the enjoyable activities he once loved because these can sometimes trigger his distress. Furthermore, he restricts his eating habits, feeling a need for control over something in his life. His body remains constantly tense and on high alert, reacting sharply to any unexpected movement nearby. This hyperarousal is part of John's heightened sense of danger, reinforcing his belief that the world is indeed perilous. Every sound or sensation can trigger his intense fear, leading him to avoid situations where he might feel vulnerable. John’s emotional numbness and shattered beliefs further compound his struggles. He feels dead inside, a stark contrast to the vibrant person he used to be. His core beliefs about safety and predictability have been irrevocably altered. The world no longer seems like a place where he can trust that things will go as planned. This sense of emotional numbness drives him to continue his maladaptive strategies, such as avoiding medical cues and restricting eating. These behaviors provide some semblance of control in an otherwise chaotic environment. His avoidance also serves as a coping mechanism for dealing with the constant triggers that remind him of his traumatic experience. John’s heightened hypervigilance has become increasingly difficult to manage over time. He finds himself scanning his surroundings constantly, which often leads to more distress and reinforces his negative beliefs about safety. This cycle of hypervigilance and avoidance has made it challenging for him to function normally at work or even in social settings with his wife. The combination of these symptoms has led John into a self-reinforcing loop where triggers intensify his maladaptive strategies, which in turn exacerbate his negative appraisals. He is caught in this vicious cycle that leaves him feeling isolated and hopeless. Despite his best efforts to manage on his own, John’s condition worsened over time. The fear of another life-threatening event, coupled with the physical discomfort, led to significant disruptions in both his work as a pilot and his personal relationships. Ultimately, it was these mounting pressures that pushed John to seek professional help. What frightens him most is the prospect of losing control entirely, leaving him feeling trapped by his own body and mind. He hopes for relief from the constant vigilance and a return to a sense of normalcy where he can feel truly safe again.
